en: // Chapter on the Objects of Cognition //
The First Daily Lesson (Āhnika)
Nyāyabindu, Pramāṇaprameya: 1. Thus, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) along with its auxiliaries has been clarified.
Now, we shall demonstrate the objects of cognition (*prameya*).
In this regard, the Vaiśeṣikas and others reflect upon categories by dividing them into groups of six, seven, and so forth.

Therefore, they themselves have admitted that those [theories] are not direct limbs of liberation. Furthermore: "Because they involve the abandonment of what exists and the acceptance of what does not exist, those delusive investigations should be excluded by those seeking liberation."
In this work, regarding the various intermediate divisions and the respective labors of reflection upon them,
we shall state only a mere indication of the faults, so as not to be overly prolix.

As for what they say there— "The referent of a word is a category (padārtha), and it is twofold, distinguished by existence and non-existence"— that is first addressed by the [sūtra]: "If it be argued that [the ether] is not [a category] because of its designation as non-existent..."

This [position] has been refuted by the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* sūtra— "Because of the mention of another entity through the remainder of the sentence and so forth, and because of another word"— which establishes that non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed a distinct positive entity (*bhāvāntara*), just like the non-existence of non-existence accepted by opponents. Furthermore,
as for the enumeration of categories of existence as being sixfold— consisting of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence— [this too is rejected].

That too has been refuted by the authors of the Sūtras themselves in the section on the Vaiśeṣikas, in the aphorism: "And because of the admission of inherence (samavāya), there would be an infinite regress due to [the resulting] equality.

Furthermore, the inference of another relation—denoted by terms such as "the relation of qualifier and qualified" or "proximity"—between non-existence and its locus is already refuted by the very same line of reasoning used to refute inherence.

And as for the category called "ultimate particularity" (viśeṣa), which is postulated as a cause—such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva)—to produce mutually exclusive cognitions among liberated selves and other things that are otherwise absolutely identical; [this too is rejected].
That [position] as well has been virtually refuted by the authors of the Sūtras on the grounds of identical reasoning.

Furthermore, by the illustration of the untenable process of atoms, dyads, and so forth in the passage, "Or like the large and long from the short and the spherical," the untenability of other [categories] accepted by them is also indicated.

Moreover, since the cognition of distinction among impermanent substances is established through genus, quality, and so forth, it is only in the case of eternal substances that another distinct category, namely *viśeṣa* (particularity), is postulated.
As they have said: "The ultimate particulars (antyaviśeṣas) reside in eternal substances.

Nevertheless, because the Vedāntins do not accept any other all-pervading category designated as "space" (dik), and because scripture declares that space is an effect, and because they reject a network of atoms distinct from the specific parts of earth and the other elements—which are themselves modifications of primordial matter (prakṛti)—such atoms [cannot be the basis for direction].
Furthermore, because the flow of states is without beginning or end, no specific distinction can be established therein;
thus, only time and the self remain as possibilities. Even so, for sentient beings, the reality of time does not manifest as their self-nature.
This is precisely because of its association with states such as moments and instants, its externality, and its insentience;
therefore, since the cognition of its distinction from itself and from others is possible,
otherwise there would follow the consequence that such a distinction could not be established even by another imagined entity.

Therefore, when the self remains as the ultimate residue, even there, since the distinction of cognitions is established through various types of differences in attributes— such as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) being atomic and all-pervasive, the governed and the governor, the contained and the container, the subordinate and the sovereign, and the body and the embodied— what further need is there for another "particularity" (viśeṣa)? For even in the case of liberated souls and eternal beings who possess extreme similarity, those particularities, established by the very means that apprehend the substratum (dharmigrāhaka), are not abandoned, so as to preserve that very state of similarity throughout the duration of the self.
Nor is there a duality of Lords, such that we would have to postulate a "particularity" (viśeṣa) for the sake of distinguishing between them as mutually exclusive;
for it is established by all the scriptures that there is only one Lord who holds sole sovereignty over all places and times.

Furthermore, since it has been established in the *Śārīraka* that this very [Self] is the subject to be expounded—according to various contexts—by means of both general and specific terms, whether through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or etymological derivation (*yoga*), and by way of its association with various particular objects and so forth;
thus, among the individual souls (*jīva*), the mutual distinction between those who are bound is made manifest by the diversity of their respective pleasures, pains, cognitions, and desires.
And the distinction between the bound and the liberated is established by such qualities as limited knowledge and omniscience, respectively.

The distinction in cognition arises precisely from the fact that purity in the case of the liberated and the eternal [entities] possesses a beginning, whereas in the case of others it is beginningless.
If it is asked, "What difference is there between the liberated state and the eternals?"—what does that matter?
For, by means of the previously perceived distinctions of qualities and so forth residing in their respective selves, the cognition of them as excluded from others is established.

Even for the Siddhas, all worldly transactions are fully accounted for by means of various previously existing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—each established by its respective means of valid cognition and maintained through recollection.
By this, the mutual distinction of cognitions among liberated beings is also explained;
for their prior transmigratory existence was not of a uniform nature.

This is because it is precisely the continuum of pleasure, pain, their causes, and so forth—characterized by specific places, times, and natures, and possessing a diversity of beginningless and incalculable karmic flows with unequal times of maturation—that serves as the mutual differentiator.

For there is no rule that the distinction between "that" and "not-that" must be established by a property existing at that very time; rather, such a distinction is established even by a property existing at another time, provided it is perceived as being inherent in that [continuum].

For the past cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is not unperceived by those who perceive the true nature of the liberated self; nor, if it were perceived, would it appear as residing in anything else. Now, what dispute can there be regarding [the nature of] eternal things?
That too is indeed skillful;

for even those whose resolutions are true possess various intentions, desires, and so forth—whose causal complexes are as unrestricted by place and time as those of Īśvara and which cannot be questioned—and these exist as beginningless and endless continuities.
What further distinction is there?
Furthermore, when a superimposition of X upon Y does not occur upon the perception of Z, that Z is indeed the difference of X from Y;
and that alone is the specific distinction (viśeṣa).
If that [distinction], being of the nature of the thing's own essence, appears in the form of "I-ness" and so forth, it would preclude the superimposition of another.
What else could that be? What then is its distinction from that [other thing]? If one does not accept this, what is the Vaiśeṣika’s recourse even if they postulate a distinction?
Those *viśeṣas* (ultimate particulars) are self-establishing and establish others.
If this is argued, are they [the particulars] themselves [the cause]?
Furthermore, if separateness (pṛthaktva) exists, what is the use of those particulars?
If it is argued that because separateness is subsumed under a single genus, there is no cognition of exclusion from it either;
In that case, it would not exist anywhere at all; or even regarding particulars (viśeṣas) that are pervaded by the nature of being particulars, what is your escape?
If you say that there is no universal (jāti) called "particularity," then what is that [particularity]?
If it is argued that [the universal] is merely an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*), why then is there no inclusion [of all individuals]?
For if that were the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the continuous cognition based upon that [attribute] would be disrupted in some instances.

Thus, the opponent’s preferred distinction—that the meaning [of the identity of cause and effect] is already established even by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and that this difficulty is insurmountable—is refuted.
Furthermore, the "universal" (*sāmānya*) asserted by others has been almost entirely rejected by the authors of the Sūtras themselves;

for instance, through such sūtras as "Its non-difference [from the cause] is established on account of the words concerning 'origination' (*ārambhaṇa*) and so forth," they show that at the stage of the effect, there is merely the attainment of a different state by the material cause.
Furthermore, by establishing that there exists no substance (*dravya*) called a "whole" (*avayavin*) as postulated by others, the absence of a whole such as a jar has been proven;

consequently, the universal "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth which would depend upon it, the qualities (*guṇa*) and other categories accepted as inherent in the whole, and the entire web of processes regarding the production of those two have been uprooted.
Moreover, that which is the distinct state of the material cause in the form of "jar-ness" and so forth—consisting of a particular conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) and the like—[is also refuted].
Since that [substance] is accepted by others as being produced and is established as such through perception and other means, there is no room for the postulation of its eternity even in that case.
Therefore, because all substances are by their very nature beginningless and endless, only the fact of their being effects, substances, and having the nature of selfhood (ātmatva), etc., remains.
Furthermore, one must consider what serves as the basis for the recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*) regarding eternal qualities and those existing in the form of states.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* and other works: “Since no object is observed that is cognized by a uniform cognition as something distinct from configuration (*saṃsthāna*), and since the conventional usage of universals such as ‘cowness’ is established by configuration alone;
furthermore, even in the theory that [the universal] is distinct [from configuration], configuration itself is admitted—therefore, configuration alone is the universal.”
"Configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is the specific form (*rūpa*) unique to each thing; thus, configuration should be understood according to the actual state of the object.

By this it is meant: Is a universal (*sāmānya*) admitted as something distinct from configuration on the basis of a clear perception of a distinct determination (*adhyavasāya*), or rather by the force of logical reasoning? It is not the first case.
The latter [alternative] is not tenable because it is unestablished,
for it is otherwise established;
for even one who accepts a distinct universal must admit that the configuration (saṃsthāna) serves as its indicator, and such a configuration is indeed observed.
If it is asked, "How can a configuration that is restricted to each individual instance be the cause of a recurring cognition?"—
or rather, "How does it become the definition of that which belongs to a certain genus?"—
if it is replied, "By way of being an adventitious attribute (upādhi) subsumed under another recurring genus," [then...]
Since the conventional usage of "cow" and so forth is established by that much alone, what is the use of anything else?
Nevertheless, in the final analysis, a recurring universal must be admitted in some cases where there is no other way to account for the phenomenon.
If you argue that otherwise even the inclusion of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) would be impossible, we ask:
in your view as well, is the universal (*sāmānya*) there included by means of a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), or not?
In the former case, there is the fallacy of circularity (*anyathāsiddhi*) and an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*).
Since no restrictive factor is observed subsequently, there would be no fixed determination of the substratum for the universal (*jāti*).
If it is argued that even among distinct individuals, there is a restriction regarding their capacity to manifest that [universal] due to their very nature (*svabhāva*),
then why does that same nature not itself regulate linguistic usage?
If it is asked, "How can there be linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) without an object (*nirviṣaya*)," [the answer is] that those very individuals (*vyakti*) are the objects.
If it is argued that if excluded things were the objects of inclusive linguistic usage, the established order of objects (*viṣayavyavasthā*) would collapse everywhere, [we reply:]...
If that which is excluded [from other things] were to manifest what is continuous [with it], why would there not be its manifestation everywhere?

If you say that this restriction is due to connection and non-connection, we say no; for since the relation called inherence (*samavāya*) is admitted to be omnipresent, one must still seek the specific rule for manifestation even in that case.
Even in the theory of various inherences (*nānāsamavāyavāda*), the restriction of the individual nature (*vyaktisvabhāvaniyama*) is difficult to abandon;
nevertheless, how could there be recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of one as "this is that" in another individual after having seen a single cow-individual?

And how could that which has been learned as the denotation of a word in one individual—such as "this is a cow"—be understood as the denotation of that same word in another individual entirely different from it?
If this is your objection, how would it be for you as well?

If you say "due to the inherence (*samavāya*) in a single property," then because you must admit that inherence— which is inherently conjoined with that very same property— subsists eternally and everywhere, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion of all linguistic conventions regarding everything in every case.

If it is argued that the restriction [of the relationship] is stated because only certain individuals possess the inherent nature of manifesting that [universal], then let those very individuals be the objects of both recognition and linguistic usage.
If it is objected that in that case, those two would be erroneous, we say no.
Because there is an absence of recognition (*pratisaṃdhāna*) and so forth as that specific individual;

if it is argued that "rather, 'being such' (*tathātva*)— which is distinct from the nature of the individual— is simply the universal (*jāti*) under another name," then why would that which manifests that universal— not being distinct from the nature of each respective individual— not be another universal?

If it is argued that this [distinction] is merely a specific limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) based on a fixed substratum, then, in that case, since the occurrence of the practice of recognition (*pratisaṃdhāna*) is possible by relying upon a mutual recollection determined by nature—which has a fixed correlative—what is the point of postulating anything else?
If it is asked, "Whence then comes the distinction between that which recalls and that which does not? [the answer follows].
Whence does the distinction between that which manifests it and that which is other than it arise?
If you say it depends on perception and non-perception, then the same applies here.
If you ask how there can be the capacity to cause recollection in the absence of a relation or similarity, [the answer is: the same applies here.
Or how [is it so] for those two?
If you say, "Because the perception of a similar thing experienced together acts as an awakener of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)," then from what does that [perception] itself arise?

If it is argued that [the capacity to remind] is postulated because the effect is observed, this is the same [for our position]; otherwise, the objection—namely, how one thing could cause the remembrance of another without relying on either a relation or a similarity—would be difficult to ward off.
Nor do we fail to accept similarity in this case.
If it is argued that because the universal is admitted to have the nature of similarity,
this is merely the acceptance of the *jāti* (universal) as intended by the opponent under a different name, [we reply]: no,
because it is precisely the excluded configurations (*saṃniveśa*) and so forth that, by their very nature of recalling specific counter-correlates, possess the form of similarity.

If it is argued that, in that case, the same would follow for the gavaya and so forth—that they too would possess the nature of belonging to the genus "cow"—we say no; for the distinction between similarity and extreme similarity is universally accepted as being based on common consensus.

Thus, when the categories such as "generality" (sāmānya) and the rest have been refuted by the authors of the Sūtras and others, certain teachers maintain that only three categories remain: substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and action (karman).

Nyāyapañcānanaprāmāṇya, verse 2: But others think as follows: "Just as those categories are rejected by the Bhāṣyakāra and others because their cognition is established otherwise, so too is action (karma).
This refers to those who maintain that action here is everywhere imperceptible—like the movement of the sun—and is to be inferred from its fruit.
In that case, let the visible fruit of action be accomplished by that very same collection of conditions through which the success of the action is intended;
what is the use of postulating an intermediate "action"? Even so, if it is nevertheless postulated:
Elsewhere as well, even when there is no perception due to a lapse in time, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating something else between the causal complex and its effect;
and since that would apply here too, there would be an infinite regress.
Furthermore, as for those who say, "the action is directly perceived,"...
We consider that even by them, upon careful examination, nothing other than conjunction and disjunction is perceived as the fruit of action;
for the cognition of "moving" is fulfilled by just that much.
Nor should it be argued that there would be the consequence of the cognition of "moving" persisting as long as the conjunction lasts.
Because that cognition has as its object the first moment of the disjunction from a preceding location and the conjunction with another subsequent location;
for it is precisely because of this that, even when a conjunction occurs at a later time, the retrospective reflection "it did not move" is logically established.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a pillar standing in the middle of a flowing stream, a disjunction from the preceding mass of water and a conjunction with the succeeding mass of water are both observed?
Nor do we admit mobility in that [stream];
if it is argued that space and so forth alone are intended as the stable locus, we say no,
because no distinction from the stream is observed there.

If it is argued that "trembling" (*laulya*) is a specific quality [of motion], then how can you deny the perception of action when trembling is perceived as a form of action distinct from conjunction and disjunction?

To this, they reply: whatever collection of causal factors for action (*karma-sāmagrī*) is accepted by you, in producing a specific conjunction intended as the result of that particular action, it produces that very [conjunction] with a restricted nature.
For this very reason, although conjunction resides in more than one thing, it produces in some cases the cognition of motion and in others the cognition of mere conjunction;

just as the single inherence, though inherently connected to both quality and substance without distinction, produces in some cases the cognition of the substratum and in others the cognition of the dependent,
for neither the state of being a substratum nor the state of being dependent is anything other than the essential nature of inherence itself.
The same applies here as well.
We, however, say this: first of all, the doctrine that action is imperceptible is untenable due to the refutations already stated;
for action, in its own nature, is perceptually evident and cannot be denied.

In this regard, one should remain indifferent [to the objection], because no additional injunctions or prohibitions are observed in the commentaries and other sources, and because there is no contradiction with other meanings.
However, we consider this: even if there were an addition, action (*karman*) does not constitute a separate category from the group of qualities (*guṇa*), as there is no differentiator.

Since a differentiator imagined according to one's own whim can be easily found everywhere, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating further groups by accepting any single quality or pair of qualities as desired;
for the internal variety of qualities does not contradict their status as qualities.
Therefore, the division is simply between "substance" (dravya) and "non-substance" (adravya).

In that regard, among those [qualities] accepted as attributes of the self— namely pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort— it has been established in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* that these five are not distinct from particular cognitions (*buddhiviśeṣa*) intended to produce them respectively. Furthermore, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are accepted as being accomplished through enjoined and prohibited actions, are— in the *Bhāṣya* and other works— of the nature of particular cognitions termed "favor" (*anugraha*) and "restraint" (*nigraha*) belonging to the Lord (*Īśvara*), the ruler of all, just as they belong to a sovereign king who possesses the power of command.
These two have been explained at length in many places.

Furthermore, that which is called "formative force" (*saṃskāra*) has been stated to consist in a particular state of the intellect (*buddhi-viśeṣa-ātman*), and it is not something produced by that [intellect].

For this reason, because pervasion cannot be observed in the case of forms that have long since perished or are remote, and because the persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is merely a matter of scriptural statement.

Nyāyapañcānana’s *Prameyakhaṇḍana*: Although, in verses of the *Gītā* such as "of each sense in its own object," the Commentator states that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the cause of activity only by way of desire, and thus there is no karma-vāsanā distinct from specific knowledge-vāsanās;
nevertheless, the existence of knowledge-vāsanā is difficult to deny.

Consequently, only its substratum (āśraya) needs to be investigated. In this regard, for those who follow the *Nyāyatattva*, *Ātmasiddhi*, *Bhāṣya*, and other works which establish that knowledge as a real entity (*dravya*), the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) called memory— which produces a modification residing in that [knowledge]— must also reside in it,
because it is internal and because there is no contradiction.
However, for those who follow the terminology of others and accept its quality (*guṇatva*) accordingly,
the impression (*saṃskāra*) resides in the self itself;
this is the distinction.

Furthermore, for those who accept both the permanence of the intellect (*buddhi*) and its various states such as contraction and expansion, it is not easy to maintain that it is not a substance (*adravyatva*);
for being the locus of different states is precisely what constitutes being a material cause (*upādānatva*),
and that alone is the defining characteristic of a substance (*dravya*).

Nevertheless, there is no loss of the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*), because we do not observe any "quality-ness" distinct from being an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*); furthermore,
we do not accept the conventional definition of a quality as that which is the substratum of a genus alone, distinct from action (*karman*).

Nor is it contradictory for a substance to have the characteristic of being dependent by nature— that is, being an inseparably established qualifier— since even you yourselves accept this in the case of a whole (*avayavin*).
And just as no contradiction is admitted [in your view] with respect to its being a substance, a qualifier, and so forth, [so too here].
Thus, it is the same here as well,
because perception, reasoning, and so forth are common to both;
therefore, cognition is a substantial entity.
Since those particular states are not substances, it is only logical that the persistence of modifications known as *saṃskāras* should reside in them alone.
Furthermore, the *saṃskāra* known as momentum (*vega*) is neither observed nor logically tenable as something distinct from the specific action intended to produce it.
However, it is more appropriate to state that elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*) is a specific kind of conjunction inseparably connected with action, even when that action has ceased.

Nyāyamañjarī, Prameyakhaṇḍa, verse 6: It is accepted that all the infinite auspicious qualities (*maṅgalaguṇa*) of the Blessed One which are proclaimed are, in fact, expansions of the sixfold set of qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
As they say: "Though You possess infinite qualities, only six are primary."
By whom even others have been placed within the womb of the world, just as by you yourself."
Thus,
among the six qualities, *bala* is the capacity for maintenance,
and *aiśvarya* is the power of control.
Vigor (*vīrya*) is the state of remaining unaltered even amidst causes of transformation;
energy (*tejas*) is the capacity to overcome others,
or independence from others.
It is evident that the four [categories] thus characterized consist of the expansion of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) in the process of thorough differentiation.
Furthermore, it is not possible to include both knowledge and power within one another in this way,
because power is observed even in insentient substances.
Because knowledge is observed even in those who lack [physical] capacity,
the claim that "capacity is a specific kind of knowledge" is thereby refuted.
If it is argued that "knowledge would instead be a specific kind of capacity," [we reply:]...

What is the meaning of the term "capacity" (śakti)? If it is argued that it is a specific quality (guṇaviśeṣa) distinct [from the substance], according to the system of Prabhākara and others, or else a separate category of entity (padārthāntara), then the status of knowledge as possessing that [capacity] as its specific quality would not be established.
Now, if you maintain that power (*śakti*) is merely a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) employed for a specific purpose, and thus conforms to all linguistic usage,
then it follows that not only cognition, but indeed everything whatsoever, would possess the status of power.
This is because [the power] exists as a qualification in whatever is considered the primary cause of everything.

If it is argued that, in this way, it follows that there is an absence of a power distinct from the essential nature and auxiliary causes— just as Udayana and others maintain— the answer is that its existence is established either by the force of reasoning that shows it cannot be explained otherwise (*ananyathāsiddhi*), or by the authority of scripture (*āgama*).
We maintain, however, that the word "that" (tat) may arise from a specific intention (*vivakṣā*).
Furthermore, the masters’ zealous effort in establishing this capacity (*śakti*) should be carefully studied in the *Nyāyakuliśa*.
And the doctrines of outsiders who assert that mere capacity (*śaktimātra*) is the cause and so forth are to be disregarded, as they lack perception, reasoning, and authoritative scripture.
If that [subtle form] were indeed grasping (*upādāna*), then it would simply be a subtle substance; thus, there is no dispute.

Now, let us examine the specific qualities of non-conscious substances (*acit-dravya*). Among these, the five beginning with sound, which reside in their respective elements, are accepted on the basis of perception and other means of valid cognition.
*Sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are accepted in accordance with the scriptures.
And conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established by perception and other means of valid cognition.
If it is argued that this [non-existence] is merely uninterruptedness,
then is that the essential nature of the substance, or is it an adventitious particular state?
Not the first, because it would entail the consequence of its being eternal;
nor the second,
because that [very thing] would be designated by a different name.
As for distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) and separation (*vibhāga*), they are to be refuted by the same logic applied to non-existence (*abhāva*).
Priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) as well are merely shadows of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth;
for we do not perceive any priority or posteriority apart from the connection with specific places and times delimited by their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
And in postulating that [quality], many other qualities such as priority (*prāktva*) and posteriority (*pratyaktva*) would likewise have to be postulated on the basis of the same logic.

Thus, by this method of demonstrating the existence and non-existence of qualities, the true nature of number, dimension, weight, fluidity, and viscidity is to be understood; such is the direction of the argument regarding non-substances (*adravya*).

Nyāyapariśuddhi, Prameya section, verse 8. Now, substances are examined. Among these, first, the doctrine of the Kaumārila school regarding a substance called "all-pervading sound" (vibhu-śabda) must be refuted, since scripture and other authorities establish that sound is a particular state of non-conscious matter (acid-avasthā).
However, in the *Ātmasiddhi*, the claim that sound transcends its substrate and possesses motion should be understood as being mediated by the parts that constitute its substratum.
As for the statement: "Darkness is indeed mobile, blue, and possessed of distinctions of priority and posteriority... [the following applies].
Because it possesses properties different from well-known substances, it deserves to be distinguished from the nine [substances].
Thus they say; we shall, for now, accept this as a substance (*dravya*).

For it has been stated by Varadaguru in the *Tattvasāra*: “We perceive that which is called ‘darkness’ as a substance, dense yet sparse, black and moving, and no sublation of it is seen by anyone anywhere.
Therefore, a cause must be postulated. Moreover, verbal cognition prevails [in this matter], for the eye reveals that [darkness] even in the absence of light, by virtue of its own perception.”
Thus,
by this [argument], the position that "darkness" (tamas) is the quality of blackness belonging to subtle particles of earth spread throughout the sky is also refuted;
for there is no contradiction in perceiving that [quality] only when it has a substrate.
Furthermore, because nothing is perceived as a mere quality in isolation,
and because touch, color, and taste— like sound and smell— are never observed to be apprehended without a substratum, whether they are erroneous or cognized through valid means;
thus, once its substantiality is established, it is appropriate to accept that a substance of black color is indeed earth.
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "That which is black belongs to food.
Although white and other colors arise on the earth due to specific modes of cooking (*pāka*), they do not arise from cooking elsewhere.
For even the perception of blueness in space and so forth arises from the contact with the earth that serves as the root of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).

This was stated in the commentary on the Sūtra, "And because there is no distinction in space": "Since the space within the cosmic egg possesses color due to the quintuplication demonstrated by the instruction on triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa), there is no contradiction in its being visible to the eye."
If it is argued that, in this way, it would follow that space itself is perceived as "dark blue" due to its contact with another substance, we reply: it would not be so,
because it is natural to perceive darkness as distinct from space, as in the expression "darkness in space."
However, [the opponent's view] is incorrect because it involves the conceptual burden (kalpanā-gaurava) of postulating a distinct substance,
and because even in this case, a conjunction with another substance is ultimately admitted through the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).
As for the non-perception of touch, it is due to its non-manifestation (anudbhava) and so forth, just as in the cases of the light of a sapphire, cloudy weather, or sunlight.
It may be so;
however, one should not postulate a rule that all terrestrial forms must necessarily be perceived by the eye in dependence upon light,
for the established order of things can be accounted for through the diversity of the sense organs as well as through the diversity of their objects.
For those who are afraid of the day and whose eyes are colored by special ointments, objects are perceived by the eye alone, regardless of light; furthermore,

if darkness were merely the absence of light, the statement regarding the cessation of both darkness and light would be contradicted, as would the effort required to postulate the imposition of a specific blueness.
Therefore, it is logical that darkness (*tamas*) is a particularity of earth.

Since the five elements beginning with earth and the mind are established by scripture and other authorities as being specific transformations of the substance consisting of the three *guṇas*, they are not distinct substances.

Furthermore, regarding the elemental substance known as a composite whole (*avayavin*), its status as something other than the [constituent] atoms is refuted by the six sūtras beginning with “The non-difference of that [effect from the cause], on account of the words concerning origin and so forth,” through the demonstration that [the existence of the composite] is otherwise accounted for by such factors as the unity of cognition and the difference in names.
This has been refuted by such arguments as, "Or like the large and the long from the short and the spherical," which address the atom (paramāṇu) as conceived by the opponent.

Therefore, it is established that the substance designated as *prakṛti* and so forth— possessing states characterized by specific transformations and by fitness or unfitness for perception— exists in the form of a manifoldly arranged aggregate and individuality, following a fixed sequence.
Even the reality of space (*dik-tattva*) consists merely of those specific locations delimited by their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
because the reasons for postulating something additional— such as the specific cognitions of "prior" and "posterior"— are otherwise established.
Furthermore, the scriptural mention of the origin of space is consistent with the creation of its limiting adjuncts and the manifestation of that which sustains them.
Otherwise, like heaven, earth, and the intermediate space, it would merely be a specific transformation of the three qualities (*triguṇa*),
and not a distinct substance (*pṛthagdravyatā*). Nor does this consequence apply to time as well.
Since eternal time has been enumerated separately by the venerable Parāśara and others,

and since the positions that it is a particular modification of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth are refuted— both because its preceding and succeeding times must necessarily exist and on the strength of the Śrutis and other authorities—
it follows that three things are established: the three qualities (*triguṇa*), time (*kāla*), and the self (*ātman*).
However, when Īśvara is enumerated separately, there are four [categories].

For although he could be included [within the category of sentient beings] due to his being conscious and so forth, he is enumerated separately by the ancient authorities to indicate his internal distinction;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of including even insentient things under a different system of classification.
And this was stated by the Blessed Parāśara: "The union of the supreme Self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality;
for this other substance is false, since one substance does not become the nature of another."

Thus, although the substance called *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as an attribute) is not distinct from [the self] in its lack of insentience (*ajaḍatva*), they nevertheless enumerate it separately on the strength of other very clear differences.
The claim by some that it is not a substance is for the most part intended merely to please others, as it contradicts the treatises of Nāthamuni, Yāmunamuni, the Commentator (Rāmānuja), and others.

Furthermore, since the existence of a distinct substance called *śuddhasattva*—established by the authoritative scriptures (*āpta-āgama*) such as the *Nirukta*, which teach the true nature of the supreme form (*paravigraha*) and so forth—is proven, positions asserting it to be a particular state of the subtle three qualities (*triguṇa*) and the like must be rejected.
Therefore, these are the six substances.

Moreover, positions asserting that the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the enjoyed (*bhogya*), and the controller (*niyantṛ*) are a single substance due to their being essentially the same "Being" (*sat*), have been refuted many times in the *Bhāṣya* and other works on the grounds of internal contradiction and opposition to scripture, just like the position of a mere undifferentiated Being (*sanmātra*).
In that context, within the pure *sattva* characterized by the three qualities (*triguṇa*),
time— consisting of moments, instants, and so forth— is defined by its own etymological derivation;
the atom is the knower, the individual soul (*jīva*).
The Lord (Īśvara) is the all-pervading one.
Intellect (mati) is the specific quality of the subject of experience, which is the uncommon cause of that experience.
Thus, the classification of substance is sixfold, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), time (kāla), the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and pure sattva-intellect (śuddhasattvamati).

Thus, for those who wish to traverse the entire range of objects of knowledge—both substantial and non-substantial—by way of this main road of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there shall be no falling into the pits of fallacious reasoning devised by those of wrong views and outsiders.

Thus ends the first Āhnika in the Prameya-adhyāya of the Nyāyapariśuddhi, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrīmad Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all systems of thought.
